us-house.budget-law-health: a budget law lowering, by roughly 14 percent over ten years, the national funding for low-income residents' public health coverage, and attaching work requirements to that coverage. Officially, roughly 3 percent of residents are estimated to lose health coverage as a result
us-house.subsidy-extension: a measure keeping the expanded premium subsidies for individually bought health insurance for three more years. Roughly 7 percent of residents have such insurance; by an independent estimate, subsidized buyers would otherwise pay more than twice as much in premiums on average
us-house.employer-plan-bill: a bill under which employer and association health plans face looser rules and money is provided for payments that lower cost sharing in individual insurance. It was officially estimated to bring pre-subsidy premiums for individual insurance down by roughly 11 percent and to leave roughly 0.03 percent fewer residents with coverage
us-house.budget-law-food: the same budget law, which in addition lowered, by roughly 16 percent over ten years, the national funding for low-income households' food assistance

uk-commons.benefit-law: a law with two parts: for four years, increases above inflation in the standard rate of the main working-age benefit, which by the government's estimate raises the income of roughly one household in seven; and a reduction of roughly half in that benefit's health-related supplement for new applicants, with no change for current recipients or for people with the most severe lifelong conditions
uk-commons.child-limit-removal: a law that ends the cap restricting child-related benefit payments to the first two children in a family. The government put the reach of the change at roughly one child in ten and estimated that it takes roughly 3 percent of all children out of poverty

de-bundestag.health-savings-law: a law to save money in health insurance, intended to keep contribution rates where they are: patients pay half as much again for medicines, spouses' free coverage under public health insurance is restricted, and payment increases for doctors, hospitals, and drug makers are held down
de-bundestag.pension-law: a pension law fixing the level of the public pension at 48 percent of average wages through 2031 and crediting parents with an extra six months of pension entitlement for every child born before 1992
de-bundestag.basic-income-reform: a reform under which the main basic income benefit, received by roughly 7 percent of residents, gave way to a stricter scheme. The rates of benefit do not change, but a person who refuses training loses 30 percent of the benefit for three months, a person who misses a second appointment has the benefit reduced for one month, and missing more appointments can end in full withdrawal

ca-commons.annual-budget-health: the annual budget, which kept the public dental plan, public drug coverage, and subsidized child care going but put no additional money into them
ca-commons.annual-budget-meals: the same annual budget, which in addition turned a national school meals program into a permanent one that reaches up to 400,000 more children a year, about 1 percent of residents

fr-assemblee.retirement-age-suspension: a law putting on hold an increase in the retirement age, which holds that age at 62 years and 9 months until 2028 and allows people born from 1964 to 1968, about 5 percent of residents, to retire three to six months earlier than planned
fr-assemblee.social-insurance-budget: the yearly social insurance budget, which included that suspension and scrapped a planned freeze on pensions and minimum benefits, letting them rise about 0.9 percent in step with prices
fr-assemblee.social-insurance-budget-health: the same yearly social insurance budget, which lifted the national ceiling for public health spending about 3 percent above the year before
fr-assemblee.negotiated-exit-benefits: a law shortening the maximum unemployment benefit period for people who end a job by mutual agreement, from 18 to 15 months below age 55 and by as much as about a quarter for older workers. Exits of this kind take more than a quarter of unemployment benefit spending, and the government's estimate of the saving was up to about 3 percent of that spending
